name: Kanarin haptic language
notes: Heard preview uses canary-like FM sweeps (2–6 kHz). Felt hardware stays at LRA resonance (~235 Hz) with the same envelopes — an Ø8 mm LRA cannot sing a bird. Play on state edge, not every sample.

science.syllable: 20–200 ms; adult repertoire ~25–40 types (Gardner et al.; Angle & Coskun).
science.phrase: Same syllable repeated ~0.5–1.5 s. Songs chain phrases; we never play a full song.
science.pitch: Most syllables 2–7 kHz, often 2.4–4.6 kHz dominant. Shapes: upsweep, downsweep, whistle, complex arch.
science.climax: Domestic canary song often ends in loud hard descending syllables (Güttinger / common description).
science.sexy: Fast FM two-note trills (~13 syllables/s) are sexually salient; we borrow the rate, not the courtship meaning.
science.calls: Contact and alarm sit outside song: shorter, used all day. Roller strains sit lower than ‘chopper’ canaries.

fridge.why: Steel door is a sounding board. Phrase must move a little metal.

wearable.why: Closer to skin. Same chirp shape, less force.

phrases.natural: Two short upsweeps — the all-day contact call, not song. ‘I’m here, look.’
A short phrase of repeated downsweeps at ~13/s — kitchen sparkle, like a busy syllable trill, not Morse dots.
Hard falling syllables — the climax of canary song, and the shape of many passerine alarms. Urgent, not pretty.
phrases.meaning: CO₂ and VOC agree — really air this

phrases.natural: One tonal falling whistle — the long, quiet syllable type, more ‘content’ than alarm. Easy to overuse.
Two tiny high upsweeps — a social chip, not a verse. Canaries peck for affection; this is the dock hello.
